title: Rehearsals, Canal Street Blues and closing thoughts on jazz
summary: The band rarely rehearsed, mostly at Lewis's yard or his house; he hopes the pioneers last and describes the brass bands at a concert.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Mm-hmm. Did you ever rehearse at any time, that band?
With the band? Yeah. Did that band rehearse?
When the voice started. What, how would you rehearse? Can you tell me about how the band rehearsed?

Well, there wasn't many rehearsals, because we, at that time, we had got kind of busy. One time we rehearsed in George Lewis' backyard. I don't know if it was down on Burgundy Street. They got the picture of it in the Look magazine. Mm-hmm. I've seen that.
You saw that. This last week they had that? Yeah. Did you get that? Did you get a copy of that?

Yeah, I had a copy of it. I don't know where the heck I put it. I got it there somewhere. Yeah, I got it there somewhere. Well, anyhow, we rehearsed there. And then we used to rehearse across the street at my house, where I was living at 825. We had more rehearsals there than we did anywhere else.
Did you ever rehearse with, using records?
No. No, except now listen to a record and try to play.
I heard that from someone that you did that on some of those tunes, maybe that you hadn't known too well, like, I can't think of the tune, Canal Street Blues or something like that.
No. I never heard that played on a recording, because we used to play that with Sidney DeVille when we was working at his club. Which one was that? The Mardi Gras.

Yeah. Well, when we was working there, we used to play that a many times with him, but we never faded off a record. But that was his favorite number, you know, that was one of the numbers that made him famous, Canal Street Blues. But, I'll say this, the fellas is passing off, the New Year's starts off kind of rough, but it's slowing up a little bit, and I hope it stays slow for a long time. Because we have quite a few pioneers left. And I'm hoping that they don't fall by the wayside, like George and Drag and Paul and several other fellas ahead of them. But anyway, they did give the world this authentic jazz music, which I'm in hopes and praying that it will stay as long as possible. Never leave. Never leave. Because I find jazz is a music that moves people. I noticed just at the concert when I was sitting behind the drums. I was thinking about how the people that were sitting out in the audience, and them bands started blasting out there, man, they forgot they were sitting out. All you could see was everybody standing up clapping. Because, you see, the bands was alternating, the brass bands. See, the onward band and the Eureka brass band. I think the Eureka brass band made a circle three times. And then the onward brass band would make a circle three times. And then one thing, they would stop in front of the bandstand, and we would play along with them. See? Well, they played like that until it was time for the closing. You know, I think they closed around about 4.30 or something like that. Then we left, and, well, they invited me upstairs, so I went on upstairs and had a drink with them. Sit down there for a while. But I must say that it was a wonderful, I think it was a better concert than last year, because if it wouldn't, if the band would have been able to march from Canal and Nels Place, I don't think all that would have went on. Because it was the bad weather that made it like that, you know, and people really enjoyed themselves. Because I've done more singing, Emma, she's done more singing than we did last year. But last year she didn't sing close or walk with me, but this year she did.
